clue.text: Lucerne detective declares his occupation

parts.note: a detective stating what he does would say 'me, dick', speaking of himself as me
dick is old slang for a detective

explanation.surface: A Swiss sleuth in Lucerne announces what he does for a living.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucerne looks like the Swiss city, but it is the fodder plant alfalfa. The detective introduces himself: 'Me? Dick', so ME comes first and DICK second.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucerne, also called alfalfa, is a species of the clover-like fodder plant genus known by this name.

clue.text: Like a particle of fish caught up in a tooth

indicators.note: the fish is caught, held inside the tooth word

parts.note: a molar is a grinding back tooth

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the fish's name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: luce is an old name for the pike

explanation.surface: A fish bone of some sort stuck in a tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns LUCE into ECUL, and 'caught' puts it inside MOLAR. Luce is an old word for a pike.
explanation.definitionFit: A molecule is a tiny particle of matter, and the adjective describes anything relating to one.

clue.text: Most of the book of words in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: only the greater part of the reference book's name is kept, cutting its final letters

parts.note: a dictionary is a book listing words

explanation.surface: Most of a reference book of words is phrased in a certain way of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' cuts ARY from DICTIONARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Diction is one's choice of words and style of enunciation when talking.

clue.text: The only one in her family to have a fit

definitions.text: The only one in her family to have a fit

parts.words: The only one in her family to have a fit
parts.note: the fairy-tale heroine was the only one of her household whose foot fitted the glass slipper; her stepsisters' feet did not

explanation.surface: A family member is uniquely prone to tantrums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have a fit' suggests a tantrum, but it means the slipper fitting her foot, unlike her stepsisters'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the pantomime tale, only the cinder-girl's foot fits the glass slipper, unlike her ugly stepsisters'.

clue.text: Mine after a month about worn out

indicators.note: the mine word follows the month word, so it goes at the end

parts.note: Dec is the abbreviation for December
re means about or concerning
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: A mine, a month later, is in a run-down state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the mine word, PIT, after the month DEC; RE (about) sits between.
explanation.definitionFit: Something decrepit is old, weakened and dilapidated through age or use.

clue.text: "A savage place! as holy and — " (Coleridge)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan, which continues the line with a word meaning under a magic spell

explanation.surface: A quotation from Coleridge with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from Kubla Khan runs 'A savage place! as holy and enchanted / As e'er beneath a waning moon was haunted'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in the Coleridge line from Kubla Khan describes a place bewitched, under a spell.

clue.text: What the horseman, it's said, did on this

definitions.text: What the horseman, it's said, did on this

parts.words: What the horseman, it's said, did on this
parts.note: the horseman rode along it, and the word for a highway sounds just like rode

explanation.surface: A riddle about what a rider did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's said' signals sound: the horseman RODE, which sounds like the thoroughfare he rode on.
explanation.definitionFit: A highway is what a rider travels along, and its name sounds the same as the past tense of ride.

clue.text: Splendid show that's mounted, one in the old city

parts.note: pomp is splendid display or ceremony

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounted means the abbreviation is read upwards

parts.note: i.e., from Latin id est, means that is
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A grand mounted parade, with one rider, in an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounted' turns IE (that is) upwards into EI. The definition is the Roman city buried by Vesuvius.
explanation.definitionFit: Pompeii was an ancient Roman town destroyed by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79.

clue.text: The North Carolina variety of fish

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so these letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: NC is the postal abbreviation for North Carolina

explanation.surface: A kind of fish found in North Carolina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' rearranges THE plus NC.
explanation.definitionFit: The tench is a European freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: Iolanthe by one other variety of fish

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Iolanthe by one other variety of fish (5)' is enumerated (5) on the scan, but the answer held is the four-letter PERI; 'other variety of fish' cannot give PERI, so the answer or clue is wrong as held.
annotationWithheld.clue: Iolanthe by one other variety of fish

clue.text: One Italian girl in fine fabric, showing gaps

indicators.note: the girl's name goes within the fabric word

parts.note: lace is a fine openwork fabric
una is Italian for one and also a girl's name

explanation.surface: An Italian girl in delicate fabric with holes in it.
explanation.walkthrough: UNA does two things: it is Italian for 'one' and a girl's name. 'in' puts it inside LACE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacunae are blanks or missing portions, as in a manuscript.

clue.text: Two blokes translating Homer?

definitions.note: the definition is a phrase describing a person, so it stands for a noun: the man who translated Homer

parts.note: chap and man are both words for a bloke
chap and man are both words for a bloke

explanation.surface: Two men working together on a Homer translation.
explanation.walkthrough: George Chapman's Elizabethan translation of Homer is the subject of Keats's sonnet 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer'.
explanation.definitionFit: George Chapman, the Elizabethan poet-dramatist, produced a famous English version of the Iliad and Odyssey.

clue.text: Musical clock I call no end fanciful

parts.note: a chimer is something that chimes, such as a musical clock

indicators.note: the word call loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A musical clock that calls out endlessly seems imaginary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' drops the final L of CALL to give CAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Chimerical means wildly imaginative or unreal, like the mythical chimera.

clue.text: In the Bible a helpmeet for a patriarch

definitions.text: In the Bible a helpmeet for a patriarch

indicators.note: the letters lie within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A Bible reference to a patriarch's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals letters held within 'BibLE A Helpmeet'; the whole clue also defines Jacob's first wife.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, the patriarch Jacob married Leah, the elder sister of Rachel, so she was his wife and helper.

clue.text: Ability to vie, catching unlimited 8

indicators.note: the rivalry verb catches, holding inside it, the trimmed fish

parts.note: to compete is to vie

indicators.note: the fish named at 8 loses its boundaries, its first and last letters

parts.note: the answer to 8 down is the fish tench

explanation.surface: The capacity to compete, by catching an unlimited number of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlimited' strips the first and last letters of TENCH (8 down) to leave ENC, and 'catching' puts it inside COMPETE.
explanation.definitionFit: Competence is the skill or capacity to do something well.

clue.text: Measure for surgeons, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: a measure is an old word for a dance, and this is a quadrille
surgeons may be those who lance boils, so this word fits them

explanation.surface: A gauge for surgeons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' means a dance here: the Lancers is a 19th-century square dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancers is a type of quadrille dance; and those who cut with a lancet, like surgeons, could be called this.

clue.text: Swell eating fish — hence extra demand

indicators.note: the swell word takes in, eats, the fish

parts.note: a surge is a swell of the sea
char is a fish of the trout family

explanation.surface: A swell of the sea swallowing a fish leads to an extra charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eating' puts CHAR inside SURGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A surcharge is an additional payment added on top of the usual price.

clue.text: Sound of a horn, also that of a bell, in London

parts.note: too means also
ting is the sound a small bell makes

explanation.surface: Horns and bells sounding in London's streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'also' gives TOO, not part of the horn sound. 'in London' adds that the answer is also a district of south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Tooting is the noise a horn makes when blown, and also the name of a district in south London.

clue.text: Nicholas Nye beginning to live in magnificent pasture

indicators.note: the donkey and the letter go within the magnificent word

parts.note: grand means magnificent
Nicholas Nye is the donkey in Walter de la Mare's poem of that name

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word live is taken

explanation.surface: A man beginning a new life in splendid pastureland.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicholas Nye, which looks like a person, is the donkey in Walter de la Mare's poem. 'beginning to' takes L from 'live', and 'in' puts ASS plus L inside GRAND.
explanation.definitionFit: Grassland is open land covered with grass, used for grazing animals.

clue.text: Like clockwork, his visits to the pub?

definitions.meaning: a pub's frequent customer is known by this word, and so are his visits

explanation.surface: His trips to the pub happen like clockwork.
explanation.walkthrough: A pub regular is a habitual customer; the clue plays on regular visits.
explanation.definitionFit: Regular means occurring at steady intervals, and also names a habitual customer of a pub.

clue.text: Design of gold on a canal-boat

indicators.note: a design is an arrangement, so these letters are laid out in a new order

explanation.surface: A golden pattern on a canal boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Design of' rearranges GOLD ON A.
explanation.definitionFit: A gondola is the long, flat-bottomed boat used on the canals of Venice.

clue.text: Insects we need to dunk right in — the drink

parts.note: to dip is to dunk

indicators.note: the letter for right goes within the drink word

parts.note: tea is the British drink

explanation.surface: Insects need dunking in the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts R inside TEA after DIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Diptera is the order of two-winged insects, including flies and mosquitoes.

clue.text: Shut up two quarters in the immediate vicinity

parts.note: east, a compass quarter, gives E
north, another compass quarter, gives N
close means nearby

explanation.surface: Two districts closed off in a nearby neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The quarters are compass points, E and N.
explanation.definitionFit: To enclose is to fence in or confine, shutting something up inside.

clue.text: Boy's optical aid

definitions.meaning: Len is a boy's name, so the possessive reads ...
a curved glass that helps one see

explanation.surface: A boy's spectacles or magnifier.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the apostrophe: LEN'S becomes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lens is a curved piece of glass that helps the eye see, as in spectacles or a magnifier.

clue.text: Something plaguey without end in the maths line

indicators.note: the insect word loses its last letter

parts.note: locusts came as one of the plagues of Egypt

explanation.surface: Something pestilential without end in a line of mathematics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without end' drops the T of LOCUST, a biblical plague.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a locus is the path or set of points satisfying a condition, often a line or curve.

clue.text: Piece of music used by Chinamen as a matter of course

definitions.meaning: a simple two-finger piano tune of this name

definitions.text: used by Chinamen as a matter of course
definitions.meaning: eating utensils used in China, where a course is a stage of a meal

explanation.surface: A tune played habitually in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as a matter of course' suggests routinely, but a course is part of a meal. 'Chinamen' is an old-fashioned word now considered offensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopsticks is a simple waltz played on the piano; the same word names the paired eating sticks used in East Asia.

clue.text: One of three aids to solution of Holmes's problem with the Reds

definitions.text: One of three aids to solution of Holmes's problem with the Reds

parts.words: One of three aids to solution of Holmes's problem with the Reds
parts.note: Sherlock Holmes calls a hard case a three-smoke problem, and the Red-Headed League case is that one

explanation.surface: Holmes needs three clues to solve the mystery of the Reds.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'The Red-Headed League', Holmes says 'It is quite a three pipe problem' and smokes for fifty minutes; the Reds are the red-headed men.
explanation.definitionFit: Holmes smokes tobacco in one while thinking, and calls the Red-Headed League case a three-of-these problem.

clue.text: No confused type of painter

parts.note: O, a nought, means nothing or no
pie is printer's slang for jumbled type

explanation.surface: No muddled sort of artist.
explanation.walkthrough: In printing, pie is type that has been mixed up. John Opie was an 18th-century Cornish painter.
explanation.definitionFit: John Opie was a Cornish portrait and history artist of the 18th century.

clue.text: One reaping harvest in the fall

definitions.meaning: to come a ... is to have a heavy fall

explanation.surface: A harvester in autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the fall' looks like American autumn, but 'come a cropper' is British for a heavy fall.
explanation.definitionFit: A cropper is someone who harvests; the word also means a heavy tumble, as in the idiom come a cropper.

clue.text: Criticize old war-time measure, bringer of many ills

parts.note: to pan is to criticize harshly
DORA was the Defence of the Realm Act, Britain's First World War emergency law

explanation.surface: Criticizing an old wartime law that brought many hardships.
explanation.walkthrough: DORA, Britain's Defence of the Realm Act of 1914, gave the government sweeping wartime powers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth, the first woman opened a jar that released all evils into the world.

clue.text: Datum line popular with bad sailors

definitions.meaning: the reference height from which heights and depths are measured
seasick sailors would like the water to stay level and calm

explanation.surface: A baseline that queasy sailors like.
explanation.walkthrough: The second part is cryptic: poor sailors prefer a level sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean sea level is the standard reference from which altitudes are measured; a flat, calm sea suits seasick sailors.

clue.text: Saw contained beryllium in the first place

indicators.note: the element's symbol goes at the front, before the holding word

parts.note: Be is the chemical symbol for beryllium
held means contained

explanation.surface: A saw that held beryllium at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the first place' puts BE before HELD.
explanation.definitionFit: Beheld is the past tense of behold, meaning to see or observe.
